readings.c1s1:
¶
'''working-out''' (wėr′king-out′), ''n.'' In ''music'', that section of a work or movement which follows the exposition of the themes and precedes their recapitulation, and which is devoted to the development of fragments, or modifications of them, in a comparatively free and unsystematic way.

'''working-party''' (wėr′king-pär″ti), ''n.'' A party of soldiers told off for mechanical or manual work, as in the repair of fortifications, or the building of a causeway or a bridge.

'''working-plan''' (wėr′king-plan), ''n.'' Same as ''working-drawing''.

'''working-point''' (wėr′king-point), ''n.'' In ''mach.'', that part of a machine at which the effect required is produced.

'''working-rod''' (wėr′king-rod), ''n.'' Same as ''pontil''.

'''work-lead''' (wėrk′led), ''n.'' [Tr. G. ''werkblei''.] In ''metal.'', the lead as it comes from the smelting-furnace, still containing a small percentage of impurities (to be removed by softening or refining) and the silver which the ore originally contained, and which is separated from the lead by pattinsonization (see ''Pattinson process'', under ''process'') and subsequent cupellation. {{smaller|The word is the literal translation of German ''Werkblei'', designating what is called in English (by Percy and others) ''blast-furnace lead''.}}

'''workless''' (wėrk′les), ''a.'' [< ''work'' + ''-less''.] '''1.''' Without work; not working; unemployed: as, a lazy, ''workless'' fellow. [Rare.]—'''2.''' Without works; not carried out or exemplified in works.
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''work-table''' (wėrk′tā″bl), ''n.'' A table or stand containing small drawers, or, in some cases, a receptacle like a work-box covered by a movable top, the whole intended for the use of women engaged in sewing. {{smaller|A common form of work-table of the last century and later had a large bag hanging from, and forming the bottom of, the lowermost drawer, or, in other words, a large work-bag made accessible by pulling out the under drawer.}}

'''workwoman''' (wėrk′wu̇m″an), ''n.''; pl. ''workwomen'' (-wim″en). A woman who does manual labor for a living: not usually applied to brain-workers. See ''workman.''

'''workyday†''' (wėrk′i-dā), ''n.'' and ''a.'' An obsolete form of ''workaday.''

'''world''' (wėrld), ''n.'' [< ME. ''world, worlde, wurld, werld, weorld, worlt, woreld, wereld, weoreld, weoruld,'' also ''word, werd, werde,'' etc., < AS. ''world, worold, woruld, weorold, weoruld'' = OS. ''werold'' = D. ''wereld'' = MLG. ''weerld, werld'' = OHG. ''weralt,'' MHG. ''werelt, werlt, welt,'' G. ''welt'' = Icel. ''veröld'' = Sw. ''verld'' = Dan. ''verden'' (for *''verlden'') (Goth. not recorded), the world, the generation of men; an orig. compound, whose elements, later merged in one and lost from view (the word, owing to the unusual conjunction of consonants, having undergone different contractions, represented by the ME. ''word,'' etc., and the G. ''welt''), are represented by AS. ''wer'' (= Goth. ''wair''), man, + ''yldo,'' age (< ''eald,'' old): see ''wer''<sup>1</sup> and ''eld, old.'' The word has taken on extended applications; the sense of ‘the earth’ is not found in AS.] '''1†.''' An age of man; a generation.

In ''music'', that section of a work or movement which follows the exposition of the themes and precedes their recapitulation, and which is devoted to the development of fragments, or modifications of them, in a comparatively free and unsystematic way.

'''working-party''' (wėr′king-pär″ti), ''n.'' A party of soldiers told off for mechanical or manual work, as in the repair of fortifications, or the building of a causeway or a bridge.

'''working-plan''' (wėr′king-plan), ''n.'' Same as ''working-drawing''.

'''working-point''' (wėr′king-point), ''n.'' In ''mach.'', that part of a machine at which the effect required is produced.

'''working-rod''' (wėr′king-rod), ''n.'' Same as ''pontil''.

'''work-lead''' (wėrk′led), ''n.''   [Tr. G. ''werkblei''.]   In ''metal.'', the lead as it comes from the smelting-furnace, still containing a small percentage of impurities (to be removed by softening or refining) and the silver which the ore originally contained, and which is separated from the lead by pattinsonization (see ''Pattinson process'', under ''process'') and subsequent cupellation. {{smaller|The word is the literal translation of German ''Werkblei'', designating what is called in English (by Percy and others) ''blast-furnace lead''.}}

'''workless''' (wėrk′les), ''a.''   [< ''work'' + ''-less''.]   '''1.''' Without work; not working; unemployed: as, a lazy, ''workless'' fellow. [Rare.]—'''2.''' Without works; not carried out or exemplified in works. {{smaller block|Ydle ''worklesse'' faith. {{right|''Sir T. More'', Works, p. 411.}}}}

'''workman''' (wėrk′man), ''n.''; pl. ''workmen'' (-men).   [< ME. ''werkman'', ''werkmon'', ''wercmon'', ''weorcman'', < AS. (ONorth.) ''wercmonn'' (= Icel. ''verkmathr''), workman; as ''work'' + ''man''.]   '''1.''' A man who is employed in manual labor, whether skilled or unskilled; a worker; a toiler; specifically, an artificer, mechanic, or artisan; a handicraftsman.

{{smaller block|Worthi is the ''werkmon'' his hure to haue.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), ii. 92.}}}}
{{smaller block|The work of the hands of the ''workman'' with the ax.
{{right|Jer. x. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>As a ''work-man'' never weary,
And all-sufficient, he his works doth carry
To happy end.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|As for matter to build with, they want none; no more doe they ''workmen''; many excellent in that Art, and those Christians, being inticed from all parts . . . to work in their Arsenals. {{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 40.}}}}
'''2.''' In general, one who works in any department of physical or mental labor; specifically, a worker considered with especial reference to his manner of or skill in work—that is, workmanship.—{{smaller|'''Employers and Workmen Act.''' See ''employer''.—'''Master workman.''' See ''master''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Workman’s candlestick,''' a simple candlestick consisting of a horizontal stem pointed at one end to be driven into a wall, and supporting at the other end a nozle or socket.}}

'''workmanlike''' (wėrk′man-līk), ''a.''   [< ''workman'' + ''-like''.]   Like or worthy of a skilful workman; hence, well-executed; skilful.

'''workmanlike''' (wėrk′man-līk), ''adv.''   [< ''workmanlike'', ''a.'']   In a workmanlike manner.

{{smaller block|They . . . doe lagge their flesh, both legges, armes, and bodies, as ''workemanlike'' as a ierkinmaker with vs pinketh a ierkin.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', III. 504.}}}}

'''workmanly''' (wėrk′man-li), ''a.''   [< ''workman'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.]   Skilful; workmanlike.
{{smaller block|In most of the houses the roofes are couered with fine gold, in a very ''workemanly'' sort.
{{right|''Webbe'', Travels (ed. Arber), p. 33.}}}}

'''workmanly''' (wėrk′man-li), ''adv.''   [< ''workmanly'', ''a.'']   In a skilful manner; in a manner worthy of a competent workman.
{{smaller block|The chappel [in Calicut] is on euery syde ful of painted deuyls; and in euery corner thereof sytteth a deuyll made of copper, and that so ''workemanly'' handeled that he semeth like flaming fire, miserably consuming the soules of men.
{{right|''R. Eden'', tr. of Sebastian Munster (First Books on America, ed. Arber, p. 17).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And at that sight shall sad Apollo weep,
So ''workmanly'' the blood and tears are drawn.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., Ind., ii. 62.}}}}
{{smaller block|A notable great Cup of siluer curiously wrought, with verses grauen in it, expressing the histories ''workmanly'' set out in the same.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 377.}}}}

'''workmanship''' (wėrk′man-ship), ''n.''   [< ME. ''werkmanshipe''; < ''workman'' + ''-ship''.]   '''1.''' The art or skill of a workman: as, his ''workmanship'' was of a high order.—'''2.''' The execution or finish shown in anything made; the quality of anything with reference to the excellence or the reverse in its construction or execution.
{{smaller block|<poem>A gorgeous girdle, curiously embost
With pearle and precious stone, worth many a marke;
Yet did the ''workmanship'' farre passe the cost.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. iv. 15.}}}}

{{smaller block|The ''workmanship'' [of sculptures of Wells Cathedral] is comparatively coarse and sketchy, and far removed from the delicacy of French carving.
{{right|''C. H. Moore'', Gothic Architecture, p. 287.}}}}
'''3.''' The product or result of the labor and skill of a workman.
{{smaller block|The mysterie of the waxe, the only ''workemanship'' of the bonie Bee, was left to lighten the Catholike Church.
{{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 352.}}}}
{{smaller block|What more reasonable than to think that, if we be God’s ''workmanship'' he shall set this mark of himself upon all reasonable creatures?
{{right|''Tillotson.''}}}}

'''workmaster''' (wėrk′mȧs″tėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' The author, designer, producer, or performer of a work, especially of a great or important work; a skilled workman or artificer.
{{smaller block|<poem>What time this worlds great ''Workmaister'' did cast
To make al things such as we now behold.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', In Honour of Beautie, l. 29.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy desire, which tends to know
The works of God, thereby to glorify
The great ''Work-master'', leads to no excess.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iii. 696.}}}}
'''2.''' A superintendent of work.
{{smaller block|<poem>A rich ''work-master'',
That never pays till Saturday night!</poem>
{{right|''Middleton'', Women Beware Women, i. 1.}}}}

'''work-mistress''' (wėrk′mis″tres), ''n.'' A female author, designer, producer, or performer of any work.
{{smaller block|Dame Nature (the mother and ''workemistrisse'' of all things).
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, xxxi. 1. (''Richardson.'')}}}}

'''work-people''' (wėrk′pē″pl), ''n.'' People engaged in work or labor, particularly in manual labor.
{{smaller block|The back-door, where servants and ''work-people'' were usually admitted.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, xiii.}}}}

'''work-roller''' (wėrk′rō″lėr), ''n.'' In a knitting-machine, a weighted roller which winds up the work automatically as it is completed.   ''E. H. Knight.''

'''workroom''' (wėrk′röm), ''n.'' A room for working in, especially one in which women are employed.

'''workshop''' (wėrk′shop), ''n.'' A shop or building where a workman, mechanic, or artificer, or a number of such, carry on their work; a place where any work or handicraft is carried on.
{{smaller block|Supreme beauty is seldom found in cottages or ''workshops.''
{{right|''Johnson'', Jour. to Western Isles, Ostig.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Workshop Regulation Act''', a British statute of 1867 (30 and 31 Vict., c. 146) which regulates the hours of labor of women and children.}}

'''worksome''' (wėrk′sum), ''a.''   [< ''work'' + ''-some.'']   Industrious; diligent.
{{smaller block|So, through seas of blood, to Equality, Frugality, ''worksome'' Blessedness, Fraternity.
{{right|''Carlyle'', French Rev., III. vi. 6.}}}}

'''work-stone''' (wėrk′stōn), ''n.'' In ''metal.'', in the ore-hearth (used in smelting lead ores), a flat plate of cast-iron connected with and sloping down from the front edge of the hearth-bottom. {{smaller|It has a raised border, and a groove running down the middle from the upper to the lower edge, down which the lead is conducted as it flows from the hearth-bottom during the reduction of the ore. Work-stones and hearth-bottoms are sometimes cast in one piece, and sometimes separately. See ''ore-hearth.''}}

'''work-table''' (wėrk′tā″bl), ''n.'' A table or stand containing small drawers, or, in some cases, a receptacle like a work-box covered by a movable top, the whole intended for the use of women engaged in sewing. {{smaller|A common form of work-table of the last century and later had a large bag hanging from, and forming the bottom of, the lowermost drawer, or, in other words, a large work-bag made accessible by pulling out the under drawer.}}

'''workwoman''' (wėrk′wu̇m″an), ''n.''; pl. ''workwomen'' (-wim″en). A woman who does manual labor for a living: not usually applied to brain-workers. See ''workman.''

'''workyday†''' (wėrk′i-dā), ''n.'' and ''a.'' An obsolete form of ''workaday.''

'''world''' (wėrld), ''n.''   [< ME. ''world, worlde, wurld, werld, weorld, worlt, woreld, wereld, weoreld, weoruld,'' also ''word, werd, werde,'' etc., < AS. ''world, worold, woruld, weorold, weoruld'' = OS. ''werold'' = D. ''wereld'' = MLG. ''weerld, werld'' = OHG. ''weralt,'' MHG. ''werelt, werlt, welt,'' G. ''welt'' = Icel. ''veröld'' = Sw. ''verld'' = Dan. ''verden'' (for *''verlden'') (Goth. not recorded), the world, the generation of men; an orig. compound, whose elements, later merged in one and lost from view (the word, owing to the unusual conjunction of consonants, having undergone different contractions, represented by the ME. ''word,'' etc., and the G. ''welt''), are represented by AS. ''wer'' (= Goth. ''wair''), man, + ''yldo,'' age (< ''eald,'' old): see ''wer''<sup>1</sup> and ''eld, old.'' The word has taken on extended applications; the sense of ‘the earth’ is not found in AS.]   '''1†.''' An age of man; a generation.

{{smaller block|If any Prince or Romane Consul did chaunce to make any lawe either necessarie or very profitable for the people, they did vse for custome to intitle that law by the name of him that did inuent and ordeine the same, for that in the ''worldes'' to come it might be knowen who was the author therof.
{{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 18.}}}}
'''2.''' Any state or sphere of existence; any wide scene of life or action: as, a future ''world;'' the ''world'' to come.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yet tell me this, will there be no slanders,
No jealousies in the other ''world;'' no ill there?</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, iv. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He tried each art, reproved each dull delay,
Allured to brighter ''worlds'', and led the way.</poem>
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Des. Vil., l. 170.}}}}
'''3.''' The system of created things; all created existences; the whole creation; the created universe: a use dating from the time when the earth was supposed to be the center and sum of everything.
{{smaller block|<poem>Par auenture ȝe haue noȝt iherde
How oure ladi went out of this ''werde.''</poem>
{{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 75.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>For god that al by-gan in gynnynge of the ''worlde'',
Ferde furst as a fust, and ȝut is, as ich leyue.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xx. 112.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ffor all the gold that euer may bee,
Ffro hethyn unto the ''worldis'' ende,
Thou bese neuer betrayede for mee.</poem>
{{right|''Thomas of Ersseldoune'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 107).}}}}
{{smaller block|All the ''world'''s a stage. ''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 7. 139.

''World'' is the great collective idea of all bodies whatever.
{{right|''Locke.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Shaftesbury conceived the relation of God to the ''World'' as that of the soul to the body.
{{right|''Fowler'', Shaftesbury and Hutcheson, p. 106.}}}}

'''4.''' The inhabitants of the earth and their concerns or interests; the human race; humanity; mankind; also, a certain section, division, or class of men considered as a separate or independent whole; a number or body of people united by a common faith, cause, aim, object, pursuit, or the like: as, the religious ''world''; the Christian ''world''; the heathen ''world''; the political, literary, or scientific ''world''; the ''world'' of letters.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then saide the iew that al this herde,
“criste, thou art sauiour of this ''werde!''”</poem>
{{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 113.}}}}
{{smaller block|One touch of nature makes the whole ''world'' kin.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., iii. 3. 175.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Philaster.'' You are abus’d, and so is she, and I.
''Dion.'' How you, my lord?
''Philaster.'' Why, all the ''world'''s abus’d
In an unjust report. ''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, iii. 1.</poem>
I have not loved the ''world'', nor the ''world'' me.
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iii. 113.}}}}
{{smaller block|There is a constant demand in the fashionable ''world'' for novelty. {{right|''Irving.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ye think the rustic cackle of your bourg
The murmur of the ''world''. ''Tennyson'', Geraint.</poem>}}

'''5.''' The earth and all created things upon it; the terraqueous globe.
{{smaller block|Men may well preven be experience and sotyle compassement of Wytte that, ȝif a man fond passages be Schippes that wolde go to serchen the ''World'', men myghte go be Schippe alle aboute the ''World'', and aboven and benethen. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 180.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>So he the ''world''
Built on circumfluous waters calm.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vii. 269.}}}}

'''6.''' That which pertains to the earth or to this present state of existence merely; secular affairs or interests; the concerns of this life, as opposed to those of the future life.
{{smaller block|Love not the ''world'', neither the things that are in the ''world''. If any man love the ''world'', the love of the Father is not in him.
{{right|1 John ii. 15.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''world'' is too much with us; late and soon,
Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Misc. Sonnets, i. 33.}}}}

'''7.''' A particular part of the globe; a large portion or division of the globe: as, the Old ''World'' (the eastern hemisphere); the New ''World'' (the western hemisphere); the Roman ''world''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Europe knows,
And all the western ''world'', what persecution
Hath rag’d in malice against us.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Perkin Warbeck, ii. 1.}}}}

'''8.''' Public life; life in society; intercourse with one’s fellows.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hence-banished is banish’d from the ''world''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iii. 3. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|Happy is she that from the ''world'' retires. {{right|''Waller''.}}}}

'''9.''' Any celestial orb or planetary body, especially considered as peopled, and as the scene of interests kindred to those of mankind.
{{smaller block|<poem>But thou shalt flourish in immortal youth,
Unhurt amidst the wars of elements,
The wreck of matter, and the crash of ''worlds''.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', Cato, v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The lucid interspace of ''world'' and ''world''.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lucretius}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
